title: Plait three cotton rope strands from a clamp: six crossings, an outer strand over the middle each time, that stay put
instruction: Plait the three rope strands from the clamp: lay an outer strand over the middle one, then the other outer strand over the new middle one, and keep alternating sides until there are six crossings. Then let go of the rope.
context: A three-strand plait is the braid most people learn first: in their own or a child's hair, in friendship bracelets and lanyards, in plaited bread, and in the rope tug toys people make for their dogs from three lengths of cotton rope. It is done the same way every time: an outer strand over the middle one, then the other outer strand over the new middle, and repeat. It is hard for a robot because the strands are soft: each must be pinched near its free end, carried over the middle strand without dragging the others along, and laid down straight on the far side so the crossing forms close to the last one. Laid slack, a strand bows near the plait, the crossings drift outward and the strands run out before the sixth; a crossing left with a short or springy tail slides off when the hand lets go. The same side twice only twists two strands together, and a strand passed under the middle makes a different braid.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left. Three 450 mm lengths of 10 mm (3/8 in) three-strand twisted cotton rope, 70 g/m (32 g each; red, natural and blue), lie flat on the bare wooden table. Their ends lie side by side, centres 11 mm apart (red on the robot's right, natural, blue), the last 15 mm of each under a steel clamp bar (34 x 60 x 9 mm, its centre at x 552, y 0) whose back is fixed on a hardwood block (26 x 60 x 21 mm, centre x 582) screwed to the table; the bar is tightened so a 50 N pull does not move an end. From the clamp's front edge (x 535) the strands run straight toward the robot in a fan: natural straight along -x to its end at x 100, red 20 degrees to the robot's right to its end near (127, -165), blue 20 degrees to the left to its end near (127, 165). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged from a top photo, which may be taken whenever both grippers are at least 3 cm from the rope and no part of the rope moves faster than 1 cm/s (on a real trial, a top-video frame with both hands 3 cm clear where the frame 1 s later shows no rope point moved 1 cm); the last such photo of the run counts (none: 0). Read the crossings from the clamp outward, tracing each strand by its colour: at a crossing the upper strand lies over (hides) the lower one. A crossing counts when an outer strand lies over the middle strand and the sides alternate (right over middle, left over middle, and so on, starting on either side). Counting stops at the first crossing that breaks the pattern: the same side twice in a row, a strand passing under the middle one, or a strand laid across both others (only its first crossing counts). A strand laid over and straight back is no crossing. Score = counted crossings / 6, at most 1.0 (six or more). If a rope end has moved in the clamp, the score is 0. The run ends early with success once photos have shown six crossings for 5 seconds in a row.
reset_notes: Unpick the plait and lay the three strands straight on their marks in the fan (a tape mark on the table at each strand's end, at the positions in the setup), ends still in the clamp. Untwist a strand if it has kinked.
fidelity: Rope at true diameter, length and mass. Each strand is a chain of 30 rigid 15 mm capsule links with bending springs, stretch and twist locked; its bending stiffness (EI 1e-4 N m^2) and the cotton friction (0.8) are estimates, and the rope's own ply twist is not modelled. The clamp holds each strand's last 15 mm fixed, so an end cannot slip. The scripted demo reads the strands' link poses; a model sees only the cameras.
